contributor_story: Born in New Orleans around 1850 at the Sazerac Coffee House, where apothecary Antoine Peychaud's proprietary bitters were mixed with Sazerac-de-Forge cognac. After the 1873 phylloxera blight wiped out French vineyards, bartenders swapped cognac for rye whiskey. It is often cited as America's first branded cocktail.

The Martini's lineage traces to the Martinez, served in 1880s Northern California, and was codified in Jerry Thomas's 1887 Bar-Tender's Guide. As vermouth ratios dropped through the early 20th century, it evolved from sweet and aromatic to the bone-dry gin icon of the mid-century. It became the definitive American cocktail of power and sophistication.

Popularized at New York's Manhattan Club in the mid-1870s, the drink paired American rye whiskey with Italian sweet vermouth and aromatic bitters. It helped launch the vermouth craze in America and became the template for the Martini and countless variations. The Waldorf's Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book later cemented its classic 2:1 ratio.

Credited to the Pendennis Club in Louisville, Kentucky in the 1880s, where bartenders honored bourbon distiller James E. Pepper. The name emerged as drinkers began asking for a whiskey cocktail made the old-fashioned way - just spirit, sugar, water and bitters - while newer cocktails grew more elaborate. It is the archetype of the original 1806 definition of the word cocktail.

Created in Florence in 1919 when Count Camillo Negroni asked bartender Fosco Scarselli at Caffe Casoni to fortify his Americano by swapping soda for gin. The equal-parts gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth formula became a global icon of the aperitivo hour. It sparked a modern craft-cocktail revival after 2000.

Named after the Daiquiri iron mines near Santiago de Cuba, where American engineer Jennings Cox mixed rum, lime, and sugar for guests around 1898. Navy medical officer Lucius Johnson brought the recipe to Washington's Army and Navy Club, spreading it through US military circles. It remains the purest expression of the sour template.

Crafted at El Floridita in Havana by Constantino Ribalaigua Vert for Ernest Hemingway, who was diabetic and demanded no sugar and double the rum. Adding grapefruit juice and maraschino liqueur, Constante produced what Hemingway called the Papa Doble. It became the template for the modern sour-with-liqueur style.

Multiple origin tales exist, but the most cited credits Carlos Herrera at Rancho La Gloria near Tijuana in 1938 for dancer Marjorie King, who was allergic to all spirits but tequila. The tequila-lime-orange liqueur formula mirrors the older Daisy template, from which its name may derive. It is now the best-selling cocktail in the United States.

Descended from the 16th-century El Draque - a mint, lime, and aguardiente remedy linked to Francis Drake's crew - the modern Mojito emerged in Havana around 1910 once Bacardi's light rum replaced rougher spirits. La Bodeguita del Medio and Hemingway's endorsement propelled it to global fame. It is Cuba's definitive highball.

Invented by bartender Fernand Petiot at Harry's New York Bar in Paris around 1921, combining newly available canned tomato juice with vodka. Petiot refined the spiced version at the King Cole Bar in New York's St. Regis after 1934, where management briefly renamed it the Red Snapper. It became the archetypal brunch and hangover cocktail.

Born in 1941 at the Cock 'n' Bull pub in Hollywood, where Smirnoff's John Martin, Cock 'n' Bull's Jack Morgan, and a partner pooled unsellable vodka, ginger beer, and copper mugs. The signature mug became essential marketing and helped ignite America's post-war vodka boom. It single-handedly mainstreamed vodka in the US.

Rooted in 18th-century Virginia as a morning medicinal, the julep entered print in 1803 and was defined with bourbon, sugar, and mint by the 1830s. Senator Henry Clay helped popularize it in Washington, and Churchill Downs made it the official drink of the Kentucky Derby in 1938. It is the South's most storied cocktail.

Created by Victor Bergeron at Trader Vic's in Oakland in 1944, reportedly for Tahitian friends who exclaimed Mai Tai-Roa Ae - out of this world. Its blend of aged Jamaican rum, orange curacao, orgeat, and lime defined the mid-century tiki movement. Don the Beachcomber disputed authorship, fueling tiki's most famous feud.

Invented by Donn Beach at Don the Beachcomber in Hollywood in 1934, reportedly to help a hungover businessman survive a meeting. Its multi-rum, fruit, and absinthe formula was so potent that the bar limited guests to two. The Zombie put tiki drinks on the American cultural map at the 1939 World's Fair.

Created around 1915 by bartender Ngiam Tong Boon at the Long Bar of Raffles Hotel in Singapore, disguising a gin sling in pink so ladies could appear to be drinking fruit juice. The original recipe was lost and later reconstructed with cherry brandy, Benedictine, and pineapple. It remains Singapore's national cocktail.

First printed in Hugo Ensslin's 1916 Recipes for Mixed Drinks, combining gin, lemon, maraschino, and creme de violette for a sky-blue hue. The violette fell out of production for decades, leaving a paler version in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy book. Its 2007 revival helped kick off the craft cocktail renaissance.

Emerged during Prohibition-era Paris around the early 1920s, when honey and lemon masked the burn of rough bathtub gin. The name is 1920s slang for something excellent. It typifies how Prohibition's poor-quality spirits forced bartenders to invent flavor-camouflaging classics.

Attributed to Harry MacElhone at Harry's New York Bar in Paris during WWI, named for the French 75mm field gun known for its kick. Gin, lemon, sugar, and Champagne produce the same artillery-grade punch. It was codified in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book.

Popularized in the early 1920s at Harry's Bar in Paris and Ciro's in London, reportedly named for an army captain who arrived at the bar in a motorcycle sidecar. Cognac, orange liqueur, and lemon form the model for the entire sour-with-liqueur family. It appeared in print in 1922 in MacElhone's ABC of Mixing Cocktails.

A rum daiquiri variant with grenadine that became so identified with the brand that a 1936 New York Supreme Court ruling required it be made with Bacardi rum specifically. It was a favorite of pre-Prohibition Americans making Havana pilgrimages. The ruling is one of cocktail history's rare legal precedents.

Invented by Henry C. Ramos at his Imperial Cabinet Saloon in New Orleans in 1888, requiring a notoriously long 12-minute shake to emulsify cream, egg white, and orange flower water. During Mardi Gras, Ramos employed dozens of shaker boys working in relay. Governor Huey Long famously flew a New Orleans bartender to New York to teach it.

Created in 1954 by Ramon Marrero at the Caribe Hilton in San Juan, enabled by the recent invention of Coco Lopez cream of coconut. It was named the official drink of Puerto Rico in 1978. Rupert Holmes's 1979 song launched it into global pop culture.

Bermuda's national drink arose after WWI when the Royal Naval officers' club blended local Gosling's Black Seal rum with ginger beer. Gosling's holds a US trademark requiring their specific rum for the name. Its stormy cloud of dark rum over golden ginger beer gave rise to the poetic name.

Rooted in the Great Tom Collins Hoax of 1874, a bar prank where patrons were sent chasing a fictional man insulting them at another saloon. Bartenders capitalized by naming a gin-lemon-soda drink after the phantom. It descends from John Collins, bartender at London's Limmer's Hotel in the early 1800s.

Born of the 1867 Merchant Shipping Act requiring lime juice aboard British vessels to prevent scurvy, combined with the navy's gin ration. Often credited to Surgeon Rear-Admiral Sir Thomas Gimlette, though the name may simply reference the boring tool. Rose's Lime Cordial, patented in 1867, made it shelf-stable for long voyages.

Created at Shoomaker's bar in Washington DC around 1883, named for lobbyist Colonel Joe Rickey who preferred his bourbon with half a lime and soda. The gin version soon eclipsed the original and became the template for Collins-style drinks. It is the official cocktail of Washington DC.

Codified in Jerry Thomas's 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide, the Whiskey Sour descends from naval grog rations of spirit, citrus, and sugar used to prevent scurvy. It is the archetype of the entire sour family of cocktails. The egg-white Boston variant emerged in the late 19th century.

Mexico's most popular tequila cocktail, likely created in mid-century Jalisco and often attributed to Don Javier Delgado Corona of La Capilla in Tequila. Its mix of tequila, lime, and grapefruit soda outsells the Margarita domestically. The name means dove in Spanish.

Invented on the page by Ian Fleming in his 1953 novel Casino Royale, where James Bond orders three measures of Gordon's, one of vodka, and half of Kina Lillet, shaken not stirred. Bond names it after double agent Vesper Lynd. Reformulations of Kina Lillet have made the original flavor nearly unreproducible today.

Brazil's national cocktail emerged around 1918 in Sao Paulo state as a folk remedy for the Spanish flu, combining cachaca with lime, sugar, and garlic. The garlic was soon dropped and the drink became a cornerstone of Brazilian social life. Its name means little countrywoman.

Created by American bartender Victor Vaughen Morris at his Morris Bar in Lima around 1922, adapting the Whiskey Sour to Peru's native pisco grape brandy. Mario Bruiget later refined the recipe with egg white and Angostura bitters. Peru and Chile still feud over ownership of both the spirit and the drink.

First printed in Harry McElhone's 1927 Barflies and Cocktails, named for expatriate Erskine Gwynne's Paris magazine The Boulevardier. Swapping the Negroni's gin for bourbon produces a richer, wintry variant. It lay forgotten until the 2000s cocktail revival rediscovered it.

Debuted at the Detroit Athletic Club around 1916 and printed in Ted Saucier's 1951 Bottoms Up. Equal parts gin, green Chartreuse, maraschino, and lime, it fell into obscurity until Seattle bartender Murray Stenson revived it in 2004. Its resurgence helped define the modern equal-parts craft cocktail era.

Codified in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, part of a family of morning-after hangover cures dating to the 19th century. Equal parts gin, Cointreau, Lillet Blanc, and lemon with an absinthe rinse create a deceptively easy-drinking bracer. Craddock warned that four in swift succession would unrevive the corpse again.

Contributed by Ernest Hemingway to the 1935 celebrity cocktail book So Red the Nose, named after his bullfighting book. A jigger of absinthe topped with cold Champagne until it turns milky opalescent, to be drunk three to five times slowly. Hemingway's instructions remain the recipe's official text.

Created by Dick Bradsell at Fred's Club in London in 1984, inspired by his childhood blackberry picking on the Isle of Wight. Gin sour with creme de mure drizzled over crushed ice became one of the first British-born modern classics. Bradsell is also credited with the Espresso Martini.

Created by Sam Ross at Milk and Honey in New York in 2005, layering blended Scotch with a smoky Islay float, honey-ginger syrup, and lemon. The drink named itself as a tongue-in-cheek cure-all. It is one of the first 21st-century cocktails to enter the modern canon.

Created by Sam Ross in 2008 for The Violet Hour in Chicago, named after the M.I.A. song Paper Planes. Equal parts bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino, and lemon produce a perfectly balanced modern sour. It became a template for the equal-parts amaro cocktails of the 2010s.

Created by Dick Bradsell at the Soho Brasserie in London in 1983 when a young model allegedly asked for something to wake her up then mess her up. Vodka, fresh espresso, and coffee liqueur became the late 20th century's definitive caffeinated cocktail. A 2010s revival made it ubiquitous once more.

Popularized by Toby Cecchini at the Odeon in New York in 1988, building on a Miami and San Francisco pink-vodka drink from earlier that decade. Citrus vodka, Cointreau, lime, and cranberry became the signature drink of Sex and the City in the late 1990s. It defined cocktail culture for a generation.

Created by Robert Butt at the Oak Beach Inn in Hampton Bays, Long Island in 1972, during a contest to invent a new drink with triple sec. Five spirits, sour, and a splash of cola disguise the potent mix as iced tea. A competing claim traces it to 1920s Prohibition Tennessee.

Invented in 1840 by oyster bar owner James Pimm in London as a digestive gin-based cordial served in tankards. The bottled No. 1 Cup launched commercially in 1859 and is still the base for the refreshing Wimbledon and Royal Ascot staple. It is inseparable from the British summer.

Evolved from the Austro-Hungarian tradition of spritzing wine with water in 19th-century Venice, with Aperol added after its 1919 invention in Padua. The modern 3-2-1 formula of prosecco, Aperol, and soda was codified in the 1950s. Campari Group's 2000s marketing push made it a global summer phenomenon.

Created by Giuseppe Cipriani at Harry's Bar in Venice between 1934 and 1948, named for the pink robe in a Giovanni Bellini painting. White peach puree and prosecco produce its signature rosy hue. It remains one of Italy's most iconic brunch cocktails.

Credited to bartender Frank Meier at the Ritz Paris in 1925, mixing equal parts Champagne and orange juice. The drink takes its name from the yellow mimosa flower. A similar Buck's Fizz was served at London's Buck's Club in 1921.

Invented during Prohibition at the Hotel Nacional in Havana and named for silent-film star Mary Pickford, who vacationed in Cuba with Douglas Fairbanks and Charlie Chaplin. Rum, pineapple, grenadine, and maraschino create a pink tropical sour. It symbolizes the American celebrity exodus to Cuba during the dry years.

A pre-Prohibition American classic of applejack, lemon or lime, and grenadine, prominently featured in Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises. The name likely refers to the rose-red color or the Jacquemot rose. It was a favorite of New York and New Jersey newspapermen in the early 20th century.

Named after the Philadelphia men's literary Clover Club that met at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel in the 1880s-1910s. Gin, lemon, raspberry syrup, and egg white create a frothy pink drink that predated the stigma against pink cocktails for men. Bartender Julie Reiner revived it in New York in 2008.

Created at Boston's Locke-Ober restaurant in 1898 to celebrate politician Martin M. Lomasney's anticipated election victory in the city's Eighth Ward. Rye, orange, lemon, and grenadine form a citrus-forward whiskey sour. It is a surviving relic of Gilded Age Boston political culture.

Named for Rudolph Valentino's 1922 bullfighting film Blood and Sand, first printed in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book. Equal parts Scotch, Cherry Heering, sweet vermouth, and orange juice produce a surprisingly balanced Scotch cocktail. It is one of the few enduring Scotch-based classics.

The original US name for the Bloody Mary when Fernand Petiot brought the recipe to New York's King Cole Bar at the St. Regis in 1934. Management thought Bloody Mary was too vulgar for its Fifth Avenue clientele. Today the name survives as the gin-based version.

Created by chef Joe Sheridan at Foynes flying boat terminal in County Limerick in 1943, to warm stranded transatlantic passengers on a bitter winter night. Travel writer Stanton Delaplane later brought it to the Buena Vista Cafe in San Francisco in 1952. The Buena Vista still serves it by the thousands daily.

Rooted in 18th-century Scotland as a mix of whisky, honey, lemon, and hot water, first printed in 1786. The name may derive from Todian water used in Edinburgh punches or Hindi tari for palm sap. It became the English-speaking world's folk remedy for winter colds.

Created by Philibert Guichet of Tujague's in New Orleans around 1918, reportedly for a New York cocktail competition where it placed second. Equal parts green creme de menthe, white creme de cacao, and cream produce its bright green hue. Tujague's still serves thousands of them each year.

A cream-added variant of the Black Russian first documented in Oakland Tribune in 1965. Vodka, coffee liqueur, and cream gained its enduring fame from The Big Lebowski in 1998, where the Dude made it his signature. Sales of Kahlua reportedly doubled after the film.

Created in 1949 by Belgian bartender Gustave Tops at the Hotel Metropole in Brussels for Perle Mesta, US ambassador to Luxembourg. Vodka and Kahlua over ice was named for Cold War connotations, not Russian origin. It remains one of the simplest two-ingredient classics.

First printed in O.H. Byron's 1884 Modern Bartender's Guide and claimed by both Martinez, California and Jerry Thomas's Occidental Hotel in San Francisco. Old Tom gin, sweet vermouth, maraschino, and bitters form the direct ancestor of the dry Martini. It bridges the 19th-century cocktail to the modern era.

Created by Joseph Santini at the Jewel of the South in New Orleans around 1852, featuring a dramatic sugar-rimmed glass lined with a full lemon peel. Brandy, orange liqueur, lemon, and bitters made it the first cocktail to use citrus juice. It is the direct ancestor of the Sidecar and Margarita.

Created by Jerry Thomas around 1860, reportedly to honor the first Japanese diplomatic mission to the United States. Cognac, orgeat, and Boker's bitters comprise the drink, which has nothing Japanese about its ingredients. It is one of the earliest documented cocktails bearing a named creator.

A late 19th-century American after-dinner drink of cognac and white creme de menthe, shaken or stirred over ice. It appears in William Boothby's 1908 World's Drinks and was the favorite of characters from Reggie Van Gleason to James Bond in Diamonds Are Forever. Its minty bite gave it the name.

Adapted by Jerry Thomas in the 1850s from a British egg-batter punch named for Pierce Egan's 1820 book Life in London, Or the Day and Night Scenes of Jerry Hawthorn and his elegant friend Corinthian Tom. Hot milk or water is whipped into egg batter with rum and brandy. It is the quintessential American Christmas cocktail of the 19th century.

Documented as early as 1695, the colonial flip was beer, rum, and sugar heated by plunging a red-hot iron loggerhead into the tankard. By the 19th century egg yolk replaced the beer, creating the modern spirit-sugar-egg template. It is one of the oldest continuously documented mixed drinks in English.

An American variant of the gin fizz using British sloe gin, a blackthorn-berry liqueur rather than a true gin. Popular in the early 20th century and revived after 2008 when Plymouth released a higher-quality sloe gin. It was a signature drink of the 1960s-70s suburban cocktail era.

Originally a gin cocktail attributed to Troy Alexander of New York's Rector's around 1915, possibly created for an advertising campaign. The brandy version eclipsed the gin original by mid-century. Cream, creme de cacao, and spirit made it one of the first dessert cocktails.

Printed in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book and attributed to Harry MacElhone of Harry's New York Bar in Paris. Brandy, rum, Cointreau, and lemon create a boozy Sidecar variant. The suggestive name made it a staple of the Jazz Age demimonde.

The gin version of the bourbon Rickey created at Shoomaker's in Washington DC for Colonel Joe Rickey, which quickly overtook the original. Gin, half a lime squeezed and dropped in, and soda water make an ungarnished, unsweetened quencher. F. Scott Fitzgerald made it Daisy's drink in The Great Gatsby.

Created in 1899 at Lake Ontario's Manitou Beach for actress Mayme Taylor, who asked for something long and refreshing after a performance. Scotch, lime, and ginger beer became a brief national sensation. It is a direct ancestor of the Moscow Mule.

Printed in George Kappeler's 1895 Modern American Drinks, combining Calvados, yellow Chartreuse, Benedictine, and Angostura. The autumnal herbal apple cocktail fell into obscurity until the 21st-century craft revival restored it. It represents the baroque layered style of the Gilded Age bar.

Printed in Jerry Thomas's 1862 guide but in use by the 1850s, featuring a sugar cube soaked in Angostura dropped into Champagne. The resulting slow bead of rising bitter bubbles makes it one of the simplest and oldest Champagne drinks. Humphrey Bogart orders it in Casablanca.

Born at Gaspare Campari's Caffe Camparino in Milan in the 1860s as the Milano-Torino, combining Milanese Campari with Torinese vermouth. It was renamed Americano during Prohibition when American visitors topped it with soda for a longer drink. It is the direct parent of the Negroni.

Created in 1732 at the Schuylkill Fishing Company, a Philadelphia fishing club considered the oldest in America. Rum, cognac, peach brandy, lemon, and tea make a deceptively smooth communal punch. George Washington reportedly became so incapacitated after drinking it that he could not write in his diary for three days.

Reputedly born in 1900 in a Havana bar when an American officer celebrating the end of the Spanish-American War toasted Por Cuba Libre over rum, Coca-Cola, and lime. Coca-Cola had only reached Havana the year before. The simple highball became a symbol of the American-Cuban relationship of the early 20th century.

Invented by Duncan Nicol at the Bank Exchange Saloon in San Francisco in the 1890s, using Peruvian pisco, pineapple, lemon, and gum syrup. Nicol took the exact recipe to his grave and Prohibition closed the saloon in 1920. Modern versions are reconstructions from former patrons' memories.

The original 1732 recipe of the Schuylkill Fishing Company, also called the State in Schuylkill. Rum, cognac, peach brandy, lemon, and sugar are stretched with tea and served from a communal bowl. It is one of the oldest continuously documented American cocktails.

Printed in Jerry Thomas's 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide, named for the old Dutch families of New York. Rum, orange curacao, raspberry syrup, and lemon make it one of the earliest American rum cocktails. It appears in nearly every major 19th-century bar manual.

Documented as the drink Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys consumed before capturing Fort Ticonderoga in 1775. Rum or whiskey combined with hard cider made a potent colonial field cocktail. It is one of the oldest recorded American mixed drinks with a historical moment attached.

An early 20th-century American highball of whiskey, ginger ale, and soda water, its austere name a joke on the temperance-minded Presbyterian Church. Often called a Press in modern bars. It was a favorite of the pre-Prohibition country club set.

A mid-century bourbon adaptation of the Moscow Mule, born as bourbon country pushed back against the vodka boom of the 1940s-50s. Bourbon, lime, and ginger beer served in the signature copper mug. It became a staple of the 2010s craft bourbon revival.

The applejack variant of the Tom Collins family, documented in early 20th-century American bar guides. Applejack, lemon, sugar, and soda served tall over ice. It represents the pre-Prohibition era when American apple brandy rivaled gin in US bars.

A Clover Club variant documented in early 20th-century American bar manuals, distinguished only by a mint-leaf garnish floated on the foam. Gin, lemon, raspberry syrup, and egg white make the pink base. The mint leaf is the sole difference from its more famous sibling.

A non-alcoholic grenadine-and-cola drink named for the RMS Queen Mary ocean liner, which began transatlantic service in 1936. It originated as a mocktail served to children and teetotalers on cruises. Its cousin the Shirley Temple was created around the same era.
